```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(svyplan)
```

Use `n_alloc_joint()` when several estimates must share one allocation of
sample across strata. A national coverage target and a regional income target
can overlap because both refer to units in the same strata. For one indicator
allocated by a classic rule such as Neyman, use `n_alloc()`. To size several
indicators under a shared design, use `n_multi()`. Use `n_cluster()` when the
allocation decision is how many units to take at each stage of a cluster design.

## Meet two targets with one allocation

Define the field strata in `frame`, the anticipated values in `measures`,
and the precision requirements in `targets`.

```{r joint-inputs}
frame <- data.frame(
  stratum = c("North urban", "North rural", "South urban"),
  region = c("North", "North", "South"),
  N = c(1000, 1800, 1200)
)
measures <- data.frame(
  stratum = rep(frame$stratum, 2),
  name = rep(c("coverage", "income"), each = 3),
  p = c(0.5, 0.4, 0.6, NA, NA, NA),
  mean = c(NA, NA, NA, 50, 55, 60),
  sd = c(NA, NA, NA, 10, 12, 15)
)
targets <- data.frame(
  name = c("coverage", "income"),
  domain = c(".overall", "region"),
  level = c(NA, "North"),
  cv = c(0.06, NA),
  moe = c(NA, 3)
)
```

`frame` contains one row per stratum. `N` counts the ultimate units on
that part of the frame. Join `measures` by `stratum` and `name`, with a row
for each indicator in every stratum its requirements cover. Supply either
a proportion `p` or a `mean` and `sd` (or `var`). Each target specifies
one metric. Here coverage needs a relative standard error (CV) of at most
0.06 overall, and mean income in the North needs a margin of error of
at most 3. Leaving the `level` column out of `targets` expands each
domain target to every level of its domain. A table that names levels, as
this one does, must name every level it targets.

```{r minimum-cost}
fit <- n_alloc_joint(frame, measures, targets = targets)
fit$detail[c("stratum", "n", "n_int")]
fit$operational$status
field <- prec_alloc_joint(fit, n = fit$detail$n_int)
field$detail[c("constraint", ".target", ".achieved", ".pass")]
```

`n` is continuous and `n_int` is the whole count to plan for in each stratum.
For this element fit, `prec_alloc_joint(fit)` checks the continuous design.
Passing `n_int` checks the field design. The pass column tests the achieved
value against the target on its own scale. Read the whole-design status
before treating its cost or precision as an optimum.

## Buy precision within a budget

Add `objective` and `budget` to minimize relative variance for the named
estimate. The same `targets` still impose hard requirements. To weight
several estimates differently, use an objective table with `name` and
`priority` columns.

```{r joint-budget}
bought <- n_alloc_joint(
  frame, measures, targets = targets, objective = "income", budget = 400
)
bought$detail[c("stratum", "n", "n_int")]
bought$operational[c("cost", "objective_value")]
frontier <- predict(bought, data.frame(budget = c(250, 300, 400, 600)))
frontier[c("budget", "cost_int", "objective_value", "cv", ".feasible")]
```

Each unit costs 1 here, so the budget is a total sample size. The
minimum-cost design above needs 268 units, and a budget of 400 spends
the remaining units where they reduce the income objective most. Along
the grid, `cv` is the CV equivalent of `objective_value`, and both fall
as the budget grows. The grid's `objective_value` describes the
continuous design. For the whole objective at a particular budget, fit
that budget and read `$operational$objective_value`, as for `bought`.

A budget of 250 cannot fund the hard targets, so its row is missing,
`.feasible` is false, and a warning gives the shortfall. A false
`.feasible` on a grid without a register can also mean the solve failed,
so read the warning for that row.

To assess a fixed allocation at different response rates, use
`predict(prec_alloc_joint(fit, n = fit$detail$n_int), ...)` with a scenario
data frame instead of predicting from the allocation itself.

## Decide how many units to take within each PSU

In a two-stage plan without a register, `N_1` counts primary sampling units
(PSUs) and `N` counts ultimate units. Costs are per PSU visit and per
ultimate unit, respectively. Give `take_2` to hold the take fixed, or leave
it out and give a range when the field team can vary the take.

```{r fixed-and-free-takes}
cluster <- data.frame(
  stratum = c("A", "B"), N = c(20000, 8000), N_1 = c(400, 160),
  cost_1 = 400, cost_2 = 40, take_2 = c(12, 8)
)
coverage <- data.frame(
  stratum = cluster$stratum, name = "coverage", p = c(0.5, 0.4), icc_1 = 0.05
)
goal <- data.frame(name = "coverage", cv = 0.10)
held <- n_alloc_joint(cluster, coverage, targets = goal)
open <- n_alloc_joint(
  transform(cluster, take_2 = NULL), coverage, targets = goal,
  take_2_min = 2, take_2_max = 20
)
held$detail[c("stratum", "n_1_int", "take_2", "n_int")]
open$detail[c("stratum", "n_1_int", "take_2_int", "n_int")]
open$operational[c("cost", "status")]
prec_alloc_joint(open, n = open$detail$n_int)$detail[c(".achieved", ".pass")]
```

The cheaper field plan can use fewer PSU visits and more ultimate units.
Supplying whole totals to the free-take assessment uses its saved whole
takes. The continuous take can differ from the take the field team uses.

## Plan from a PSU register

Replace `N_1` with a register table. Give each PSU its stratum and size
`N`, with sizes summing to the stratum's ultimate-unit total. Keep
`psu_id` to match the planned takes and zones back to the register. The
default `fpc` setting is required for this register model.

```{r zoned-register}
register <- data.frame(stratum = "A", psu_id = seq_len(100), N = 1000)
zoned <- n_alloc_joint(
  data.frame(stratum = "A", N = sum(register$N), take_2 = 10),
  coverage[1, ], targets = transform(goal, cv = 0.08),
  psu = register, n_psu_per_zone = 2
)
zoned$detail[c("n_psu_certain", "n_psu_draw", "n_zone", "n_int")]
head(zoned$psu[c("psu_id", "certainty", "take_2", ".zone")])
prec_alloc_joint(zoned)$detail[c(".achieved", ".pass")]
design_df(zoned)
```

This equal-size register draws 24 PSUs across 12 zones. Certainty PSUs
are included automatically when the design calls for them or when the
input register flags them. On a remainder row, `take_2` is the take
if the PSU is drawn. The field plan's draw counts and zones tell the
sampling team how many PSUs to select. The plan's `stages` is 2, and
`prec_alloc_joint(zoned)` assesses the stored field design directly.
For a raw register assessment, supply the stratum totals to assess as
`n` and put the fixed `take_2` in `frame`. See `?merge_psus` when
the frame needs to combine small neighboring PSUs before planning.
